nominations.abstract: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.

nominations.title: Time-Specific Multinomial Logistic Regression for Competing Risks
nominations.authors: Haoxuan (Charlie), Zhou (Joan), Xiaoqiong (Joan), Hu, Yi Xiong, Yan Yuan
nominations.abstract: Motivated by the project on premature menopause among childhood cancer survivors in the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS), we develop methods for estimating time-specific factor effects using doubly censored event time data with competing risks. We begin with fitting separate binary logistic regression models for different causes. However, the approach does not ensure the sum of the resulting estimated cumulative incidence rates remains bounded by one. To overcome this limitation, we consider a multinomial logistic regression formulation to jointly model all cause-specific risks. Two inverse-probability-of-censoring-weight (IPCW) based estimating functions are proposed accordingly. To handle the estimation instability caused by data separation, we incorporate the Firth-type penalization in those estimating functions to obtain more stable coefficient estimators. The sandwich variance estimator is applied to estimate the standard errors. A weighted quasi-likelihood information criterion, paired with a backward elimination, is further adapted to the proposed estimating functions for selecting covariates at a given age. Simulation studies are conducted to examine the proposed approaches regarding consistency, efficiency, and robustness of the estimators. The Firth correction substantially reduces the bias induced by separation and provides valid standard error estimation. We illustrate the proposed approach with the CCSS data viewing premature ovarian insufficiency and surgical premature menopause as the two potential causes of the primary event, premature menopause. The data analysis reveals that the effects of the cancer treatment-related covariates are significant on premature ovarian insufficiency but not on surgical premature menopause. The variable selection procedure, illustrated on an extended covariate set, yields estimated risks close to those under the full model.

nominations.title: Robust Inference for Spiked Eigenspace under Elliptical Distributions
nominations.authors: Zeyu Wang, Qing Yang, Xiao Han
nominations.abstract: In this paper, we study two eigenspace testing problems under high-dimensional elliptical spiked models: whether the spiked eigenspace equals a given subspace, and whether a given vector is a spike eigenvector. We propose a \textbf{Robust Functional Projection} (RFP) test and a \textbf{Robust Spike Direction} (RSD) test for these two problems, respectively. Based on the spatial-sign covariance matrix $\bm C_n$, both tests achieve robustness by remaining invariant to the radial distribution without moment conditions and allowing the background level to be unknown. To construct and analyze both tests, we establish central limit theorems for \textbf{G}eneralized \textbf{E}lliptical \textbf{S}patial-sign \textbf{S}pectral statistics (GESS) $\operatorname{tr}\{f(\bm C_n)\bm B_n\}$. The results cover a general class of deterministic weighting matrices $\bm B_n$ whose ranks are either comparable to the dimension or of smaller order, providing a common theoretical foundation for both tests. The central idea in constructing both tests is to avoid the need for consistent estimations of individual spike eigenvalues by working directly with GESS. Simulations illustrate the finite-sample performance of the procedures, and an analysis of LOCATA acoustic data demonstrates their use in assessing a signal subspace and a steering direction, both constructed from measured source and array geometry.

nominations.title: Characterizing Estimator-Regime Transitions in Adaptive Enrichment Trials
nominations.authors: Xin Luo, Maria Kudela, Margaret Gamalo
nominations.abstract: Adaptive enrichment trials that identify responsive subpopulations allocate a fixed sample across them and estimate each one's effect from the resulting data. For a synthetic control design with adaptive recruitment and borrowing of control outcomes, we ask whether a doubly robust family of targeted maximum likelihood estimators should replace its sample mean; the choice can be made largely at the design stage. A crossing condition weighs the bias removed and the efficiency gained by the doubly robust family against the finite-sample inflation of nuisance estimation; an equal-error boundary, located by simulation, separates the families in the plane of sample size and bias. A consistency principle prices recruiting with the wrong family's variance functional. With three and eight simulated subpopulations the boundary's sign prediction for the mean squared error difference holds in $99.6\%$ of $10{,}302$ comparisons decided at two standard errors. A pre-specified selector commits to the doubly robust family where the squared anticipated bias exceeds the net variance term. Recruiting along that family's path costs up to $0.035$ in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; recruiting with the sample mean functional and routing only the analysis removes this cost and about nine tenths of its error excess.

nominations.title: Efficient Causal Survival Inference under Limited Surrogate Monitoring
nominations.authors: Zhenyue Du, Weishang Kong, Wei Li
nominations.abstract: Post-treatment surrogate endpoints can improve the efficiency of causal survival effect estimation, but their monitoring may end before follow-up for the primary outcome. We investigate the impact of limited recurrence monitoring on semiparametric efficiency when mortality follow-up continues. We derive the efficient influence function under limited monitoring and establish an exact expression for the efficiency gain from extending monitoring between any two durations. Our framework encompasses the absence of surrogate information and the usual shared-censoring scheme as boundary cases, and allows comparison with fully observed surrogates. We develop a doubly robust estimator under limited surrogate monitoring and establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency for its cross-fitted version under suitable conditions. Simulations and an application to breast cancer data illustrate the proposed method.

nominations.title: Movement based social interactions with label uncertainty
nominations.authors: Anisha J. Mathias, John W. Durban, Holly Fearnbach, Samantha G. M. Leander, Henry R. Scharf
nominations.abstract: Drone-based imagery provides high resolution data for tracking wildlife populations. However, monitoring marine mammals like cetaceans is challenging because individuals frequently submerge into water or move out of the drone's field of view, resulting in disconnected trajectories due to uncertain identities. Existing social movement models assume individual identities are known, which is often only true when data come from physical tracking devices like GPS collars. To address this limitation, we propose a Bayesian hierarchical state-space model that treats the identities associated with observed locations as unknown random variables. This allows us to jointly estimate individual movement parameters while propagating the uncertainty about identity. We apply our framework to drone-measured movement data from Risso's dolphins (Grampus griseus) to estimate the effects of sonar exposure on the dolphins' movement behavior. Our proposed method offers a solution for analyzing collective animal behavior when continuous tracking of every individual is challenging.

nominations.title: Sharp Design-based Inference for Quantiles of Individual Treatment Effects
nominations.authors: Jiangchuan Du, Xinran Li
nominations.abstract: Understanding the distribution of individual treatment effects (ITEs) is a central problem in causal inference. In general, however, this distribution is only partially identifiable from observed data because it depends on the unidentifiable joint distribution of the two potential outcomes. In this paper, we develop design-based inference for the distribution of ITEs whose validity relies solely on the randomization of treatment assignment, treating the potential outcomes as arbitrary fixed constants. Building on recent randomization tests for ITE quantiles, we propose tests based on either a rank-based Kolmogorov--Smirnov (KS) statistic or the usual KS statistic, with the latter being more conservative in the presence of ties. We show that, under certain regularity conditions, the confidence bounds obtained by test inversion are asymptotically no worse than the sharp bounds on ITE quantiles given the marginal distributions of the potential outcomes. We further derive a closed-form expression for the confidence bounds from the KS-based randomization test and show that they can be equivalently constructed by combining sharp bounds on ITE quantiles with uncertainty of empirical marginal distributions. This equivalence connects randomization-based inference with partial identification and clarifies the special role of the KS statistic in achieving sharp inference. Under additional distributional assumptions, we characterize the power of the proposed randomization tests under local alternatives. Finally, we discuss how to incorporate covariates to further sharpen inference. We illustrate the properties of the proposed methods using both simulations and a real-data application.

nominations.title: Nonnegativity Shapes Predictive Uncertainty: Complementary Model Fits and Quantile Construction
nominations.authors: Jialin Li
nominations.abstract: Knowing that a response cannot be negative can inform predictive uncertainty, including extreme upper quantiles. This knowledge matters especially when a black-box system returns long vector responses at few covariate settings, leaving large uncertainty across many entries. We develop a framework that assembles predictive distributions feature by feature from distributional fits that incorporate nonnegativity, optionally around any given mean predictor. The fits come from a latent factor model that represents response intensity through nonnegative patterns whose amplitudes follow rectified Gaussian processes over covariates. A variational algorithm jointly learns the factorization and the latent posterior. Varying a conditional-dispersion parameter yields a spectrum of fits that show complementary strengths in estimating distributional shape features. An orthogonal quantile expansion motivates using L-moments or their ratios as features. We select a fit separately for each using scores computable from a single validation observation per entry, then assemble the selected estimates through the expansion. In simulations, this construction reduces extreme upper-quantile errors by 17-22% relative to the respective best single fit, despite the mode-seeking tendency of our variational inference. In a streamflow demonstration across agricultural catchments, using an external point simulation to supply the mean reduces miss rates of rare shortage by 86-91%.

nominations.title: Estimating Average Treatment Effects with Projected Instrumental Variables
nominations.authors: Shuyuan Chen, Yifan Cui
nominations.abstract: In this paper, we develop a projected instrumental variable framework that relaxes conventional assumptions for causal identification with instrumental variables. Building on the interpretation of conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the framework replaces the conditional expectation operator with a general projection operator. We provide an alternative inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation. Drawing on semiparametric efficiency theory, we further develop debiased and adaptive machine learning methods for estimation and inference. The proposed framework connects invalid instrumental variables to instrumented difference-in-differences. We also examine invalid projected instrumental variables and discuss their relationship to existing methods. Simulation studies and real data analysis demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably compared with existing approaches.

nominations.title: Causal Record Linkage
nominations.authors: Kayan\'e Robach, Michel H Hof, Mark A van de Wiel, St\'ephanie L van der Pas
nominations.abstract: Combining observations from multiple data sources creates a valuable resource for research. In causal inference, record linkage methods grant researchers access to the covariates needed for unbiased estimation and offer the means to explore (long-term) outcomes. This paper examines how record linkage conflicts with the assumptions required for identifying causal effects. Our investigation reveals that linkage errors primarily threaten consistency in the causal framework, leading to attenuation bias in the inference due to discrepancies in the linked data. In attempting to address this bias by being more stringent on the linkage, sampling bias inadvertently emerges from a covariate shift between the baseline and the linked samples, as profiles with more distinctive information are more likely to be recovered. Despite these challenges, we identify settings in which record linkage and causal inference can be soundly combined, and show how the effect estimated on linked data can be generalised, with linkage decisions informed accordingly. We further identify when existing and novel solutions support valid causal inference on linked data, and when inference should instead be treated with caution or even abandoned. We illustrate the challenges raised and the potential solutions using real data from a study of women's health and a simulation study.

nominations.title: Finite-Sample Calibration and Power Benchmarks in Two-Sample Random-Integration Tests
nominations.authors: Pengfei Wang
nominations.abstract: In high-dimensional two-group studies, a supplied variable set can be used directly or to learn a projection. We study how much attainable power these choices retain at fixed observation and calibration budgets. For complete unbiased random-integration statistics under Gaussian common shape, a fixed-spectrum comparison orders direction-wise power and gives an explicit criterion balancing an oracle advantage against learning loss. Joint regeneration controls level for a specified learner with unknown diagonal shape. A paired construction permits observation reuse and finite-reference calibration of fitted scores and menus. In the paired diagonal experiment, an invariant sparse likelihood-ratio benchmark provides an attainable efficiency target. Finite-amplitude bounds connect a classical bounded quadratic to this target; conditioning on the coordinate maximum yields informative complementary bounds at moderate and strong signals. Both comparisons include finite reference budgets, and null-only simulations certify local comparisons with specified fitted rules. Equal-budget experiments and a leukemia application compare aggregation, projection and fitted quadratic scores. For correlated paired data, classical sign randomization supplies a separate calibration under central symmetry. The efficiency guarantees apply to the stated experiments and signal classes; general small-budget shape efficiency and adaptation to unknown signal allocation remain open.

nominations.title: Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality
nominations.authors: Jiahe Li, Jerome P. Reiter
nominations.abstract: The mean log deviation and the Theil index are two widely used measures of income inequality. The organization releasing these measures may be obligated to protect the confidentiality of the individual incomes used in the computations. In particular, the organization may wish to release versions of these measures with formal guarantees of privacy. The organization could do so by satisfying differential privacy; however, typical applications of differentially private algorithms are likely to add so much noise to the measures that they become unusable. We present differentially private algorithms for these indices with reasonable error properties. The algorithms rely on computing or approximating bounds on the smooth sensitivity, that is, the maximum absolute amount the inequality measures change when replacing any subset of the $n$ incomes in the reported data with arbitrarily chosen feasible values. For the mean log deviation, the algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time. For the Theil index, the algorithm runs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We illustrate the performance of each differentially private algorithm using individual-level and household-level income data from the Current Population Survey. We also examine repeated sampling properties of the algorithms using artificially generated data. The empirical results indicate when these differentially private algorithms can be expected to provide accurate estimates and when they are likely to introduce too much noise.

nominations.title: Deformed Q-learning for High-Dimensional Dynamic Treatment Regimes
nominations.authors: Ming Cheng, Zhao Chen, Christina Dan Wang
nominations.abstract: In high-dimensional dynamic treatment regimes, nonlinear terminal outcome models complicate upstream conditional-mean modeling and inference based on recursively estimated continuation values. We introduce a Deformed Q-learning procedure for general action spaces that accommodates a terminal-stage GLM, random designs, conditional heteroscedasticity, and fine-grained action discretization. The procedure changes the recursive criterion by propagating the terminal deformed optimal Q-function through sparse block-wise linear conditional-mean models. Under the stated models and regularity conditions, we establish consistent and asymptotically normal estimators, accounting for downstream estimation uncertainty in inference for optimal Q-values, deformed optimal Q-values, and their contrasts. We bound population regret relative to the original terminal mean-outcome objective without explicit stage-wise accumulation. Estimation and inference also extend to a growing number of stages under conditions uniform across stages. Simulation studies demonstrate accurate estimation and variable selection. In an empirical application to sepsis management using the MIMIC-III database, the proposed framework supports stage-specific value inference, while an auxiliary action-alignment analysis provides an exploratory signal that early-stage concordance with the learned recommendation may be associated with improved survival.

nominations.title: A Bayesian Magnitude-Composition Model for Tree-Size Distributions and Stand-Tables
nominations.authors: Andrew O. Finley, Malcolm S. Itter, Arthur Spitta, Arne Nothdurft
nominations.abstract: Sparse forest inventories often provide too few plots to estimate species-specific tree-size distributions for individual stands. We develop a general Bayesian magnitude-composition model that separates overall abundance from its allocation among categories. A negative-binomial model describes total counts, while multinomial models describe how those counts are allocated among categories. In forest inventory, this construction allocates trees among species and then size classes within species, without imposing a parametric form on the tree-size distribution. Covariates inform both abundance and composition. Shared latent factors represent residual spatial and group-level dependence among categories using relatively few processes, while smoothing priors on regression coefficients borrow information across neighboring size classes. Nearest-neighbor Gaussian processes support efficient spatial computation. Joint posterior prediction and area-weighted aggregation yield stand-tables---tree densities by species and size class---and derived measures such as size-class diversity, with associated uncertainty. Simulations show small estimation errors and near-nominal predictive-interval coverage for forest and stand summaries. An application combining field plots and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) covariates illustrates estimation of species-specific distributions of diameter at breast height and size-class diversity in sampled and unsampled stands.

nominations.title: High-Frequency Estimation of the Leverage Effect under Rough Volatility with Microstructure Noise
nominations.authors: Zhao Chen, Ming Cheng, Christina Dan Wang, Ziyang Xiong
nominations.abstract: This paper develops feasible high-frequency inference for the leverage effect when the spot variance follows rough Volterra dynamics, leverage loadings depend on endogenous rough states, and observed prices may be contaminated by microstructure noise. We define an integrated leverage parameter through a scaled covariation between log prices and spot variance that accounts for their different local fluctuation scales. The scaled realized covariation admits a stable functional central limit theorem with an explicit pathwise centering correction arising from within-interval variation in the leverage loading. A loading regularity condition renders this correction asymptotically negligible, and we verify the condition for direct Volterra loadings and for smooth functions of closed rough states for every Hurst index below one half. We construct a block-based estimator with an exact finite-window correction for the leading proportional bias, together with a nonnegative single-scale estimator of its asymptotic variance. Pre-averaging extends feasible inference to observations with independent and identically distributed microstructure noise. Simulations under the rough Heston model demonstrate accurate finite-sample calibration with and without noise. An empirical application to fifteen years of one-second data on nine U.S. equities and ETFs finds negative median leverage estimates for every asset at weekly and monthly horizons.

nominations.title: Second-Order Least Squares Method for Statistical Inference in Linear Models with Asymmetric Errors
nominations.authors: Sanha Kil, Yuliya V. Martsynyuk, Liqun Wang
nominations.abstract: In a linear regression model with normal random errors, the ordinary least squares estimator is the most efficient estimator. However, when the random errors have an asymmetric distribution, a more efficient estimator can be constructed using the higher moments of the data. In this paper, we use the second-order least squares method to obtain more accurate asymptotic confidence intervals and more powerful hypothesis tests in linear models. We also develop an efficient and stable numerical algorithm to calculate the proposed estimator. Our extensive simulation studies demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method. Two real data examples are presented.

nominations.title: Inference in an interactive multi-type branching network
nominations.authors: Gunay Hasanli, Michel Mandjes, Jiesen Wang
nominations.abstract: We study statistical inference for a high-dimensional stochastic interaction model observed only through low-dimensional aggregate data. The model describes pairwise communication between $d$ individuals as a collection of mutually interacting branching processes with immigration, where activity on one directed pair may trigger subsequent activity in the reverse direction. The latent interaction counts are not observed. Instead, for each individual, only the total number of messages sent and received in each time slot is available. This aggregation gives rise to an inverse problem in which the parameters governing the latent pairwise dynamics must be recovered from substantially compressed observations.

nominations.title: Mutual Information Estimation via Triangular Transport Maps: Finite Sample Guarantees and Sample Allocation
nominations.authors: Fengyi Li
nominations.abstract: We study finite sample guarantees for transport based mutual information estimation. Mutual information can be estimated by first learning the conditional and marginal densities and then evaluating their log-density ratio by Monte Carlo. Given training samples, we use triangular transport maps to learn these densities and then compute the mutual information estimate on an independent batch of evaluation samples. For conditional density estimation using triangular transport maps, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees over realizable H\"older classes by viewing the conditional density as an ordinary density with respect to the product of the law of the conditioning variable and Lebesgue measure. This allows standard density estimation techniques to be applied directly to the conditional density estimation. These results yield finite sample guarantees for the resulting mutual information estimator and characterize how a fixed sample budget should be allocated between training and evaluation in order to minimize the mean squared error. Numerical experiments support the predicted training and evaluation error rates and illustrate the resulting sample allocation tradeoff.

nominations.title: Unconstrained support points can leave a convex support
nominations.authors: Zhaohui Li
nominations.abstract: Support points provide a practical and effective way to approximate a probability distribution by a small set of equally weighted representatives through energy-distance minimization. In many applications, the variables satisfy convex constraints that the representatives should also respect. We investigate whether unconstrained support points automatically satisfy such constraints and show that this is not guaranteed. We construct counterexamples using three planar observations, a density with full triangular support, and positive-definite matrix data admitting an indefinite optimal representative under the Frobenius norm. We also identify cases in which containment holds, establish stability under distributional perturbations, and quantify the objective cost of imposing a convex-hull constraint. For a fixed number of representatives and a positive population constraint gap, empirical configurations with vanishing global objective error eventually leave the sample convex hull almost surely.

nominations.title: The Statistical Geometry of Latent Recovery in Hidden Markov Models
nominations.authors: Trang Pham, Dung Le, Alessandro Rinaldo, Nhat Ho
nominations.abstract: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) offer an important capability to interpret fitted latent states and transitions. When emission distributions nearly coincide, a small observation-density error does not ensure accurate estimation of the latent quantities needed for interpretation. This motivates us to characterize convergence rates for latent recovery that account for emission separation. Our main contribution lies in deriving deterministic inverse inequalities that convert Hellinger error between fitted and true densities into bounds on latent recovery errors. We develop these bounds for multivariate Gaussian HMMs with a common, known emission covariance matrix and combine them with a Hellinger estimation guarantee for the global maximum likelihood estimator to obtain latent recovery rates. Although the joint observation distribution is a Gaussian mixture with exponentially many path components, they share the same emission centers across time. Leveraging this shared structure, we show that the separation exponents are governed by the maximum number of simultaneously approaching centers rather than the number of path components. Under exact specification, the global bounds on state-sequence probability discrepancies and the 1-Wasserstein loss for latent location distributions exhibit sharp separation exponents that do not increase with the number of selected times. Moreover, sufficiently small observation-density error guarantees unique matching between fitted and true emission centers, which yields error bounds for individual emission centers and transition rows. Under over-specification, individual split-state transition rows are not necessarily identifiable, so we quantify aggregate latent recovery errors and show that state-sequence probability bounds incur larger separation exponents compared to exact specification. We conduct synthetic experiments to validate our theoretical results.

nominations.title: Martingalized U-statistics-based sequential inference: a blessing of degeneracy
nominations.authors: Weijia Li, Leheng Cai, Qirui Hu
nominations.abstract: Degenerate degree-two U-statistics have non-Gaussian limits, making sequential inference substantially more difficult than in the nondegenerate case. However, row normalization preserves the target parameter and makes the centered numerator a martingale on a harmonic variance clock, at the cost of logarithmic variance inflation. We establish a strong Gaussian approximation for this process and consistently estimate its variance through online updates, allowing spectrum-free calibration. Combining this strong approximation with Gaussian-mixture (GM) and stitched law-of-the-iterated-logarithm (LIL) boundaries yields confidence sequences with asymptotic time-uniform coverage and corresponding sequential tests for null hypotheses under which the kernel is degenerate. We further extend the framework to multi-dimensional vector-valued kernels, yielding Mahalanobis confidence ellipsoids based on consistent covariance estimation. Numerical experiments illustrate sequential type-I error control and favorable detection power in two-sample and independence testing against spectral baselines, and in three-sample homogeneity testing using vector confidence ellipsoids.

nominations.title: A semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises theorem at rate $n^{-3/2}$ for frequency estimation
nominations.authors: Paulo Serra
nominations.abstract: We consider Bayesian inference for the frequency of a periodic signal of unknown shape, observed in Gaussian white noise on the interval $[0,n]$. The information about the frequency grows like $n^3$, so the frequency can be estimated at rate $n^{-3/2}$, while the shape is an infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter. We endow the frequency and the shape with independent priors, the prior on the shape being a random series in the trigonometric basis. We give conditions on the priors under which the posterior for the signal contracts at a rate that, for suitable choices, is the minimax rate for Sobolev classes of smoothness at least one, up to a logarithmic factor and adaptively to the smoothness of the shape. If, moreover, the prior keeps the shape away from shapes with a shorter period, also the marginal posteriors for the frequency and the shape contract around the truth. Under further conditions, which hold for a Gaussian random series prior conditioned to keep the shape away from shapes with a shorter period, for every true shape with smallest period 1 and Sobolev smoothness larger than $3/2$, the marginal posterior for the frequency satisfies a semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises theorem at rate $n^{-3/2}$, which we prove by moving the origin of time, a change that leaves the posterior unchanged when the prior on the shape is invariant under time shifts.

nominations.title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
nominations.authors: Gengyu Xue, Fan Wang, Feiyu Jiang, Zifeng Zhao, Yi Yu
nominations.abstract: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

nominations.title: Unlikely likelihoods: likelihood analysis for the triangular and random histogram models
nominations.authors: Nils Lid Hjort
nominations.abstract: This paper concerns certain parametric models for densities on the unit interval which lead to nonsmooth and nonregular likelihood functions. (i) The first is the simple triangular model on the unit interval, characterised by a density linearly increasing from zero to the mode position $\theta$ and then linearly decreasing to zero from the mode to one. With data from this model the likelihood function is a sum of individually log-convex terms, and with the derivative having discontinuities at each data point. (ii) The second is the one-parameter two-box density which is flat on $[0,\theta]$ and $(\theta,1]$, with $\theta$ the median. The likelihood has jumps at each datapoint. Here the maximum likelihood estimator is sharper than usual, with convergence in distribution of $n(\hat\theta-\theta)$ to a nonnormal limit. We also study the $k$-box extension of this model, with density being flat on $k$ boxes determined by $k$ quantiles. (iii) This second model is extended to the two-parameter two-box model, with areas $\gamma$ and $1-\gamma$ for boxes $[0,\theta]$ and $(\theta,1]$. Again the likelihood is nonregular, and the maximum likelihood estimators exhibit different rates of convergence for the breakpoints and the density values. The model generalises to the $2(k-1)$ parameter density piecewise flat over $k$ boxes. For each of these models we tend to the delicate task of sorting out the large-sample behaviour of the log-likelihoods, then leading to precise and partly nonstandard limit distributions for the maximum likelihood and Bayes estimators.

nominations.title: Sharp Critical Rates for Locally Private Distribution Estimation
nominations.authors: Yi Liu, Xiaotian Chang, Qirui Hu
nominations.abstract: We determine sharp minimax rates for distribution estimation under pure local differential privacy at critical query smoothness. For the integral probability metric generated by the unit ball of $B^d_{2,q}$, $1\le q\le\infty$, over fixed periodic Sobolev density balls with positive smoothness and interior slack at the uniform density, the expected risk is of order $N^{-1/2}(\log N)^{3/2-1/q}$, where $N=n\varepsilon^2$; expected squared risk has the squared order. The fine index governs aggregation across resolutions that share one private information budget. A single noninteractive release with a measurable proper density output attains these rates, and matching lower bounds allow finite public blackboard interaction and repeated participation under each user's total privacy budget. A known $L^2$ radius permits the same rates without using density smoothness, with output in the $L^2$ density ball. Separately, for positive smooth densities on $[0,1]$, integrated squared CDF risk has minimax order $(\log N)^2/N$, with sharp quantile, Wasserstein, and transport map consequences. The rates hold uniformly for $0<\varepsilon\le1$ as $N\to\infty$, with class parameters fixed.

nominations.title: Minimax estimation of linear functionals in the Darcy inverse problem
nominations.authors: Yi Liu, Xiaotian Chang, Qirui Hu
nominations.abstract: We study estimation of linear functionals $\int f\psi$ of the conductivity $f$ in the Darcy problem $\nabla\cdot(f\nabla u)=g$ from observations of $u$ in Gaussian white noise of level $N^{-1/2}$. When the potential has a single nondegenerate minimum, we determine the minimax rates over Sobolev balls in the linearised experiment. Unless a compatibility condition along the gradient flow holds, the rate is governed by an effective dimension $T$ of the Hessian at the minimum, not by the ambient dimension: it is $N^{-(2s+T)/(4s+8)}$ for $T<4$, has an elbow at $T=4$ with an extra logarithmic factor, and is parametric for $T>4$. In the nonlinear experiment we show that these lower bounds persist when compatibility fails at the reference and $T\le4$, and we prove the minimax rate on classes with isotropic critical Hessians, and the parametric rate near references with $T>4$. In dimension at most four, no nonzero linear functional is uniformly $\sqrt N$-estimable on a Sobolev neighbourhood of the constant conductivity, even when it is regular there.

nominations.title: Optimal Certified Multiple Testing with E-values
nominations.authors: Soumyabrata Bose, Jay Bartroff
nominations.abstract: We study randomized multiple testing with e-values under arbitrary dependence and introduce a conditional certification constraint: Given the observed evidence, each coordinate's expected rejection certificate must not exceed its e-value. Existing randomized e-BH improvements satisfy this constraint but have no established optimality guarantee. We prove that the maximum conditional inclusion probability for hypothesis $i$, given e-values~$x$, is $1 \wedge (\alpha / K) \sum_j \min(x_i, x_j)$, and construct one rule attaining these bounds simultaneously. The rule uses a single independent uniform variable, rejects a prefix of the ordered e-values, and has a unique conditional rejection-set law among rules attaining all the bounds. It therefore maximizes every nonnegative weighted sum of inclusion probabilities, including expected true discoveries under any truth configuration. Under a shared uniform draw, its rejection set contains those of e-BH and U-eBH. The construction extends to BY-calibrated p-values, and simulations under positive and negative dependence show power gains over existing randomized procedures.

nominations.title: A unified study of explosive processes with a root in the neighborhood of the unit circle
nominations.authors: Marie Badreau, Fr\'ed\'eric Pro\"ia
nominations.abstract: This study is dedicated to autoregressive processes with stable and explosive time-varying coefficients, with a particular emphasis on a root located inside or outside the unit circle but converging towards the unit circle as the sample size increases (so that the limit process is integrated). Our objective is to develop a unified asymptotic theory that connects the classical stable, unstable and explosive regimes. By considering roots approaching the unit circle from both the stationary and explosive sides, we investigate how the corresponding asymptotic behaviors (of the process and the OLS) interact, and we try to build bridges between the rates associated with these regimes. This perspective provides a framework for understanding mixed autoregressive dynamics having a root in the neighborhood of the unit circle, provided a fairly general set of conditions.

nominations.title: Moment-Orthogonal Quadratic-Envelope E-Processes for Anytime-Valid Location Inference
nominations.authors: Serhii Zabolotnii
nominations.abstract: E-process confidence sequences for unbounded means typically use a variance bound and a first-order score, leaving skewness and kurtosis unused. We construct a quadratic-envelope e-process from a conditionally centered vector score with a predictable second-moment bound. Under moment information specified independently of the tested stream, it stays positive on unbounded support and gives exact anytime-valid coverage under predictable strategies and fixed mixtures, without score clipping. For a location family with known central moments through order four, the centered observation and its centered square yield an exact confidence sequence whose local width shrinks, relative to a first-order construction, by a factor determined by skewness and kurtosis. At level 5%, the largest null ever-crossing rate was 4.63%; on two zero-inflated-lognormal families median stopping times fell by 36.8-45.8%. When the moments are calibrated on an independent reference sample, a centering-robust factor keeps exact coverage at a closed-form width cost: the median gain was 21.6-30.3% for Gamma(2) and lognormal errors with 10^6 reference observations, and a loss of up to 9.9% with 10^4. On public Fermi gamma-ray detector data with a declared stability margin, it crossed at the current location in 1.8% of 225 windows and stopped 30-35% earlier than the calibrated first-order method.

nominations.title: Sharp upper and lower bounds on the variance of U-statistics
nominations.authors: Kiarash Nikoo, Liqian Zhang, Dennis Leung
nominations.abstract: For a U-statistic with a symmetric kernel of any rank, we offer new upper and lower bounds on its variance, which are uniformly sharper than those established in the classical paper by Hoeffding (1948, Theorem 5.2). Our new bounds have strong optimality properties and can tightly describe how the variance scales with the degree of the kernel. As an application, we leverage our new upper bound to improve an existing Berry-Esseen theorem for the normal approximation of incomplete U-statistics based on Bernoulli sampling, in a computationally frugal regime where the computational budget is much smaller than the available sample size.

nominations.title: Federated Estimation of Loading Spaces in Tensor Factor Models under Differential Privacy
nominations.authors: Zetai Cen, Fan Wang, Haeran Cho
nominations.abstract: Tensor factor models provide low-dimensional representations of tensor-valued observations while preserving their multiway structure. When these observations are held by different clients, privacy constraints may prevent them from being pooled for centralized analysis. We study estimation of common loading spaces in Tucker tensor factor models under federated differential privacy, allowing heterogeneous sample sizes, privacy budgets, and factor strengths. The proposed method combines private stability testing, Huber aggregation, and Gaussian perturbation at each client with weighted aggregation at the server. We establish non-asymptotic upper bounds governed by a scaled harmonic mean of the squared local error rates, and prove minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors under strong factors, fixed factor ranks, and fixed noise variance. We further develop a private calibration procedure that selects the local tuning parameters and aggregation weights without knowledge of the noise level or client-specific factor strengths. The resulting adaptive estimator preserves the privacy guarantee and attains the error rate obtained with oracle tuning. We illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators through simulation experiments and an application to a Meditation Traits EEG dataset.

nominations.title: Asymptotic delta-like behavior of the weighted taper in Thomson's multitaper F-test
nominations.authors: Hau-Tieng Wu
nominations.abstract: We study the weighted taper arising in Thomson's multitaper F test, which is constructed from pre-plunge discrete prolate spheroidal wave functions (DPSWF). Numerical evidence suggests that, in the asymptotic regime, the Fourier transform of this taper converges to a delta measure supported at the origin. We provide a rigorous theoretical justification for this behavior.

nominations.title: Randomized Adaptive Sequential Allocation and the Limits of Bounded Exposure to Inferior Treatments
nominations.authors: Sampurna Kundu, Monitirtha Dey, Atanu Biswas
nominations.abstract: A clinical trial must learn which treatment is superior while sparing its participants from the inferior one. Kundu et al. 2025 recently showed that a purely deterministic rule, which always assigns the treatment with the larger current sample mean, achieves a strong form of this ethical goal. The smaller allocation count stays almost surely finite and has all moments bounded uniformly in the sample size. Deterministic allocation is, however, predictable, and predictability invites selection bias. We ask whether this bounded-exposure phenomenon survives once the deterministic rule is replaced by a smooth randomized one. We show that it does not. Under any fixed non-degenerate symmetric randomization, both treatments are sampled infinitely often, the adaptive sample means are strongly consistent, and the inferior treatment draws a strictly positive limiting allocation proportion. Consequently, the inferior allocation count grows linearly and its moments are unbounded. We then study annealed randomization, in which the randomization scale cools with the accumulated information, and obtain summability and divergence criteria that separate finite, sublinear, and linear exposure. A forced-exploration variant identifies the superior treatment with probability one while keeping the inferior exposure sublinear, and thereby frees the annealed guarantees from any correct-stabilization event. We also treat normalized multi-treatment rules, ties, indifference zones, unequal variances, general response distributions, and local alternatives. Finally, we develop the post-trial asymptotic inference that each exposure regime permits. The results delineate the trade-off between allocation concealment, persistent exploration, and ethical concentration on the superior treatment.

nominations.title: Beyond least-favorable distribution pairs: asymptotically instance-optimal robust hypothesis testing
nominations.authors: Aytijhya Saha, Aaditya Ramdas
nominations.abstract: When testing a composite null $\mathcal{P}$ against a composite alternative $\mathcal{Q}$, it has been known since Huber and Strassen (1973) that if a least favorable distribution (LFD) pair exists, then a version of its likelihood ratio yields a minimax optimal test, and Huber (1965) derived a similar result in the sequential setting for a specific robust testing problem that is the focus of the current paper; the same likelihood ratio is log-optimal in the worst case; its expected logarithm under the alternative equals $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P},S \in \mathcal{Q}} KL(S\|P)$, whose inverse also determines the stopping time of the test under the alternative. These results focus on optimizing worst-case performance, but the resulting methods have lower power if the data come from simpler alternatives. This paper studies an arguably more practical goal of achieving asymptotic \emph{instance optimality} for ``power-one'' sequential tests, which remarkably may even be possible when $\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{P}^c$. This means that when the data are drawn from any $S \in \mathcal{P}^c$, the test has power one, and its stopping time is determined by the larger information number $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}} KL(S\|P)$, which governs the performance of an oracle that knows $S$. To demonstrate this point, our paper focuses on the case of testing a TV ball around a discrete distribution with $d$ components, and designs a computationally and memory efficient algorithm that is also asymptotically instance-optimal. Specifically, we consider two different asymptotic settings: one is the "Wald setting", where the type-1 error level $\alpha$ approaches zero for a fixed alternative $S$ and the second is the "Farrell setting", where $\alpha$ is fixed and $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}} KL(S\|P)$ approaches $0$. Our sequential test is simultaneously optimal in both regimes.

nominations.title: On the Conditional Consistency of the Bootstrap
nominations.authors: Denis Kojevnikov
nominations.abstract: This paper focuses on the conditional consistency of the bootstrap. The target is the conditional law of a statistic given a common shock, and the bootstrap approximates it by the law of a resampled statistic conditional on the shock and the data. We call the bootstrap consistent if these laws are close in the Kolmogorov distance for almost every realization of the shock. The conditioning $\sigma$-algebras are allowed to be unrelated across sample sizes, and both the comparison law and the dimension of the data may vary with the sample size. We give sufficient conditions for consistency in this sense, show that they yield asymptotically correct conditional coverage for bootstrap quantiles, and provide a finite-sample bound on the coverage error. We also relate the Kolmogorov formulation to the merging of probability measures. The results are specialized to statistics depending smoothly on an estimator or on an estimated nuisance parameter.

nominations.title: $P$-stationary structural equation modeling: Causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations
nominations.authors: Nicolas-Domenic Reiter
nominations.abstract: Causal modeling of discrete-time processes often involves the assumption that the modeled processes are stationary. A general class of linear causal models for discrete-time stationary processes are structural equation processes (SEP), which generalize the well known structural equation model for i.i.d. observations. In this paper, we extend the SEP model from stationary to $P$-stationary processes, which are non-stationary processes whose $P$-periodically sampled subprocesses are jointly stationary. We will use this model to approach the problem of causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations from a graphical modeling perspective. To have a notion of generic identifiability, we restrict our analysis to $P$-stationary structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) processes, which are SVAR processes whose underlying coefficients can vary $P$-periodically over time. Our findings allow to detect, in any given temporally incomplete observational setting, if a certain set of instrumental processes qualifies to identify a causal effect between $P$-periodic subprocesses, and if this is the case, that effect admits an explicit expression as a rational function evaluated at the observational spectral density.

nominations.title: Robustness of Median-based Splitting Rules for Causal Trees
nominations.authors: Karolina Gliszczy\'nska-Schroeder, Jens Klenke
nominations.abstract: Causal forests (Athey and Imbens, 2016) are a widely used method for the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects. Standard implementations use mean-based splitting criteria, which perform well when the outcome distribution is well-behaved and free of contamination, such as outliers or heavy tails. However, real-world data are rarely clean. Outcome perturbations can affect the tree structure selected by mean-based splitting rules and lead to unreliable treatment effect estimates. In this study, we systematically examine the robustness of causal forests to irregularities in the outcome distribution. Building on the median-based splitting criteria introduced by Ma{\ss}mann and Gliszczy\'nska-Schroeder (2026), we empirically investigate three median-based splitting criteria: Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), Least Median of Squares (LMS), and Median Squared Deviation (MSD). We conduct Monte Carlo experiments and apply the methods to empirical benchmark datasets from the causal inference literature to compare the performance of the median-based approaches with standard causal forests. We additionally examine pointwise confidence interval coverage using the Bootstrap of Little Bags and the infinitesimal jackknife. The results indicate that median-based splitting criteria can reduce sensitivity to outcome irregularities in specific scenarios, particularly in the presence of extreme heavy-tailed noise and nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity. However, these benefits are scenario-dependent and do not consistently lead to more accurate conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.

nominations.title: When Does $N$ Buy Precision? Heterogeneous Responses to Aggregate Shocks in Micro Panels
nominations.authors: Mahmut Ablay, Mengshan Xu, Endong Wang
nominations.abstract: Panel local projections (panel LPs), valued for their flexibility and robustness, are widely used to estimate heterogeneous responses to aggregate shocks from micro data. This paper, however, highlights the potential of panel vector autoregressions (panel VARs) and characterizes the trade-off between the efficiency of panel VARs and the robustness of panel LPs. In contrast to existing results in the time-series literature, we show that under correct specification, panel VAR estimators of the heterogeneous responses converge at rate $(NT)^{-1/2}$, whereas panel LP estimators converge at rate $T^{-1/2}$. When the heterogeneous response function is nonparametric, the panel VAR incurs a nonparametric rate loss, whereas the panel LP retains its parametric $T^{-1/2}$ rate under suitable smoothness and panel-growth conditions. We provide a Hausman-type test for choosing between them, with power against two forms of panel VAR misspecification. We apply panel LPs and panel VARs to Turkish administrative firm-level data to estimate heterogeneous firm responses to monetary policy shocks.

nominations.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
nominations.authors: Irene Aldridge
nominations.abstract: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $\beta/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $\Theta((s/\beta)^2\log(1/\delta))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

nominations.title: Testing Exogeneity in Nonparametric Instrumental Variable Models
nominations.authors: Xiaojun Song, Jichao Yuan
nominations.abstract: We propose a test of mean exogeneity in nonparametric instrumental variable models. Under completeness, the null is equivalent to a conditional moment restriction involving the ordinary regression function, so the test avoids estimation of the structural function and its ill-posed inverse problem. We construct a residual-marked empirical process and analyze it through an auxiliary U-process of order two. We derive its limiting distributions under the null and Pitman-type local alternatives of order $n^{-1/2}$, and establish consistency against fixed global alternatives. The analysis reveals a nonparametric estimation effect that invalidates a direct multiplier bootstrap. We propose a computationally simple multiplier bootstrap with a tailor-made indicator correction to account for this effect, and establish its asymptotic validity. Simulations show good size control and power gains over existing methods in the nonparametric designs considered. An application to a wage equation provides evidence against the mean exogeneity of schooling.

nominations.title: Exploiting Locally Exogeneous Variation in Spatial Data: Linear Regression with Many Small Units
nominations.authors: Christopher W. Engh
nominations.abstract: This article shows how researchers can exploit \textit{locally exogeneous variation} even in the presence of endogeneity, autocorrelation, or spurious correlation. It describes the infill asymptotic properties of generalized least squares estimation with county-level data, Census tract-level data, and similar regional averages, including sufficient conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality, and valid inference.

nominations.title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk
nominations.authors: Jiuyi Cheng, Alexis Akira Toda
nominations.abstract: Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined.

nominations.title: Looking Forward to Constructing Better Causal Comparisons
nominations.authors: Augusto Cerqua
nominations.abstract: Constructing credible comparison groups is a central challenge in observational causal inference. Conventional approaches assess comparability through observed characteristics or pre-treatment outcome trajectories, although causal identification depends on unobserved untreated potential outcomes after treatment. We propose a forward-looking framework that selects or weights controls using prognostic scores: predictions, based on pre-treatment information, of the outcomes units would experience without treatment. These scores target either untreated outcome levels or changes, depending on the comparability condition underlying the causal design. They can be estimated using post-treatment outcomes observed for untreated units or exclusively from historical data. To construct these scores, we leverage tabular foundation models, whose extensive pretraining enables them to capture complex relationships among predictors and effectively extract their predictive information, even when application-specific samples are limited. Crucially, predictions guide comparison-group construction, whereas observed outcomes determine treatment effect estimates. We derive an exact decomposition of estimation error into prognostic-score imbalance and differences in forecast errors, clarifying why neither predictive accuracy nor score balance alone guarantees causal identification. The National Supported Work application reveals that stronger pre-treatment covariate balance does not necessarily yield estimates closer to experimental benchmarks, highlighting the practical relevance of prognostic-score comparisons.

nominations.title: Selective Randomization Inference for Interference
nominations.authors: Takahide Yanagi
nominations.abstract: Empirical researchers often use tests for interference as pretests or robustness checks. However, when the results guide the choice of models, parameters, or hypotheses, the resulting data-dependent selection can compromise the validity of subsequent inference. This paper develops a two-stage selective randomization inference framework for interference that explicitly conditions on the selection event to account for data-dependent selection. We first test the null hypothesis of no treatment spillover using a conditional randomization method. If this null is rejected, we test the null hypothesis of zero exposure contrast under a pre-specified exposure mapping that allows for spillover effects; otherwise, we test the null hypothesis of no direct effects under the assumption of no spillover. We prove that each second-stage test controls the selective Type I error rate in finite samples and evaluate the size and power of the proposed tests through Monte Carlo experiments.

nominations.title: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk: Semiparametric estimation and inference
nominations.authors: Yuhan Ma, Heng Peng, Feipeng Zhang
nominations.abstract: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk (EVaR) has attracted increasing attention in financial risk management owing to its desirable theoretical properties. However, existing estimation methods for conditional EVaR either rely on potentially misspecified parametric models or suffer from the curse of dimensionality in nonparametric approaches. To this end, we study semiparametric estimation and inference for conditional EVaR in nonlinear time series models with unspecified error distribution. Specifically, we propose a two-step conditional EVaR estimator that achieves the parametric convergence rate. Furthermore, we derive a functional central limit theorem for conditional EVaR process, and then extend to investigate estimating both conditional expectile-based expected shortfall and conditional distribution. A residual bootstrap procedure is proposed for non-expert practitioners to conduct statistical inference. The asymptotic results and their applications are illustrated by numerical studies and an empirical application to S\&P 500 returns.

nominations.title: Sharp Fr\'echet--Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation
nominations.authors: Rami V. Tabri
nominations.abstract: Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fr\'echet--Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

nominations.title: When Covariates Mask Pre-Trends
nominations.authors: Parush Arora
nominations.abstract: Honest difference-in-differences methods judge how far parallel trends may fail after treatment by how far it failed before treatment, as shown by placebo estimates. When the design adjusts for covariates, the placebo estimates are adjusted too. We show that this benchmark is valid only if the covariates are measured before the earliest placebo window. A covariate measured later already reflects shocks to the outcome during the placebo period, so adjusting for it hides part of the pre-trend. The placebos then look flatter than the true trend and the resulting confidence sets are too narrow. When the covariate is also observed at an early date, the distortion can be estimated and tested. Of 90 recent published studies that adjust for time-varying covariates, 77 measure at least one covariate too late.

nominations.title: Sharp Identification for Regression with Interval-Observed and Missing Covariates
nominations.authors: Martin Fankhauser, Gil Jan Peled
nominations.abstract: Researchers frequently estimate regressions when key variables are missing or observed only through intervals. Imputation or assumptions about the observation process can yield seemingly precise but misleading conclusions. We develop methods for identification and inference that remain robust to such incomplete data. For a broad class of conditional moment models, we characterize the sharp identified set, the set of all parameter values consistent with the observed data and maintained regression model, without restricting how incomplete observations arise. We establish Hausdorff-consistent estimation and uniformly valid confidence regions, and develop computationally tractable implementations for common regression models. In an application relating interval-elicited discount rates to on-time high-school graduation, conventional inference excludes zero, whereas our interval-data-robust confidence regions include it. Exploiting sharp identification nevertheless yields substantially tighter confidence regions than non-sharp alternatives.

nominations.title: Unconfoundedness as an Information Constraint
nominations.authors: Christoph Breunig
nominations.abstract: This paper provides an information-theoretic characterization of unconfoundedness within a general class of models allowing for endogenous selection. We impose a conditional mutual information (CMI) restriction requiring that the information about treatment contained in a potential outcome, conditional on covariates, does not exceed that contained in its latent heterogeneity. Under the maintained model conditions, this restriction is equivalent to a multiplicative factorization of treatment probabilities into separate functions of latent heterogeneity and covariates. Although the CMI restriction permits endogenous selection, sufficiently rich variation in treatment probabilities across covariate values makes it equivalent to unconfoundedness for the corresponding potential outcome. For binary treatments, any nonconstant propensity score suffices; for multiple treatments, a full-rank condition on the second-moment matrix of the propensity-score vector is sufficient. State-specific restrictions bound residual selection and imply exogeneity for individual treatment states under boundary-support conditions. Extensions cover continuous treatments and instrument exogeneity.

nominations.title: Validating LLM-Generated Synthetic Survey Samples: A Use-Dependent Multi-Dimensional Framework for Social-Science Applications
nominations.authors: Enrico Angelo Raffaele D'Ecclesiis, Fulvio Castellacci, Arash Ahmadi
nominations.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) make it increasingly feasible to generate synthetic survey respondents, but their empirical usefulness cannot be judged by a single notion of accuracy. A synthetic sample may perform weakly at the respondent level while still preserving distributional or substantive relationships relevant to social-science analysis. We develop a use-dependent, multi-dimensional validation framework distinguishing predictive, distributional, and substantive validity, and illustrate it using Eurobarometer data on attitudes toward artificial intelligence. Four off-the-shelf LLMs generate responses conditional on observed respondent profiles, while supervised machine learning provides a predictive reference for interpreting their performance. The results reveal substantial differences across validation dimensions: some LLM-generated samples preserve meaningful marginal heterogeneity, demographic ordering, cross-country variation, and predictor structure despite imperfect respondent-level correspondence. Performance varies across models and outcomes, but the broader picture is cautiously constructive. Synthetic samples should therefore be evaluated against the empirical properties required by their intended use.

nominations.title: Accessibility to Higher Education and Inter-regional Mobility
nominations.authors: Se-il Mun, Shun Fujita, Lei Qin
nominations.abstract: We develop an equilibrium model of the undergraduate higher education market that incorporates interregional mobility for enrollment. An individual chooses a college to attend, seeking to maximize utility depending on the quality of education and the costs of attendance. Costs include tuition fees, the effort required to pass the entrance exam, and moving costs from one's hometown to the region where the college is located. Each college admits students whose entrance exam scores exceed a certain threshold, which we call the college's qualifying score. In our model, the qualifying score of each college is determined endogenously as the shadow price of the constraint that the number of enrolled students must not exceed capacity. We structurally estimate the model's parameters by simulating equilibrium using Japanese data. Based on empirical results and counterfactual experiments, we evaluate the welfare costs of disparities in access to higher education due to uneven spatial distribution of colleges among regions.

nominations.title: Dynamic investment in disaster preparedness under recurrent and catastrophic risks
nominations.authors: Tomoki Ishikura, Muneta Yokomatsu
nominations.abstract: Long-term disaster risk reduction (DRR) requires investment decisions that account for uncertain disaster conditions and accumulated preparedness capacity. This study develops a novel stochastic dynamic control model for optimal DRR investment under recurrent and catastrophic uncertainty. The model combines diffusion and Poisson jump processes and treats preparedness capital as an endogenous stock that accumulates through investment, depreciates, and mitigates economic damage. We derive a state-dependent investment rule from the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation to minimize expected discounted investment expenditure and disaster damage over an infinite horizon. Monte Carlo policy comparisons and numerical experiments examine how disaster risk structures interact with investment decisions to shape preparedness accumulation and economic losses. The results show that the economic value of DRR investment depends on adjustment to evolving conditions and disaster loss mechanisms. Lower expenditure can coexist with greater preparedness, while similar expected losses can conceal different upper-tail risks. Effective investment therefore requires attention to both accumulated preparedness and the structure of disaster risk. These findings support long-term DRR planning that integrates investment timing, capital maintenance, and recovery conditions with residual loss assessment. Upper-tail indicators complement expected-loss evaluation without being directly optimized. The framework provides a basis for dynamically managing preparedness capital.

nominations.title: Learning about Markets from Models: Evidence from an AI Hiring Platform
nominations.authors: Hossein Alidaee, Tarun Khanna, Rembrand Koning
nominations.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used to not only inform, but make decisions. Sometimes platforms add value by pooling data across contexts to improve models' decision making---but when the optimal decision differs by context, pooling may not increase accuracy. We argue that a platform storing starkly distinct models across contexts nevertheless captures a model comparison externality. Together, these models reflect how decision makers respond differently to the same data in the current equilibrium. Policymakers can use this differentiation to prioritize interventions; firms can learn how they are already differentiated from competitors to focus future investments. Our evidence comes from an AI hiring platform used by large employers of low-skill workers. The platform uses a standardized psychometric assessment to create firm-specific models estimating each application's retention likelihood at that firm. Each firm's model is highly predictive for itself but no better than chance at other firms. We use these models to create a firm-application matrix: each firm scores each application, not only the ones it receives. An application's improved retention likelihood if submitted to a different firm is highly heterogeneous based on traits. Further, these gains are due to two distinct mechanisms. Finally, firms value traits differently even in this low skill market: they disagree about whether important traits improve or worsen retention at the margin. These insights are only possible when a platform can access both the full application pool and each firm-specific model. We explain the value of these insights to firms, policymakers, and platforms.

nominations.title: An analytical model to explain under which conditions home batteries create new load peaks in the local grid
nominations.authors: Lion Hirth
nominations.abstract: Simulation studies find that price-responsive home batteries and electric vehicles create new load peaks in low-voltage grids; with endogenous wholesale prices most of these peaks disappear. This paper explains both findings with an analytical model of the coincident peak at the transformer. The model is algebraic and solved in closed form, so the parameters that determine whether a new peak emerges and how large it becomes can be identified; they are few. The peak is the background load in the critical hour plus the charging of the local fleet. Under exogenous prices the charging equals the rated power of the fleet. Under endogenous prices the national fleet fills the trough of residual load until the price is flat; the depth of the fill follows from an energy balance in which the price function does not appear. For a V-shaped trough the local charging peak is the share of the grid in national flexibility times the square root of flank gradient times national flexibility. Rated power, price level, network charge and market size do not enter. The model reproduces simulated peaks for a German case within a few percent.

nominations.title: Floods and the Duplication of Production: Evidence from the Global Car Industry
nominations.authors: Michele Fioretti, Sophia Praetorius, Thierry Mayer
nominations.abstract: Floods are becoming more frequent and can disrupt global supply chains. We study how multinational car makers adapt vehicle and key parts production to flood risk, and how their choices interact with insurance and public flood defences. Using plant-level data and a manually verified flood record in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that car makers duplicate production rather than move it away from flooded plants. Even more than five years after a flood, an engine is 19 percentage points more likely to be made in two or more plants, usually abroad and for cars assembled nearby, while the flooded plant's output shows no persistent decline beyond a temporary loss in the flood year. Firms duplicate only where adjustment costs are low, i.e. when a plant of theirs abroad already makes the same engine family. Flooded vehicle model versions are duplicated only temporarily, and transmission programs are not duplicated. Suggestive evidence that firms duplicate more where insurance is likely expensive and plants lack flood defences points to substitution between redundancy, insurance and public protection.

nominations.title: The Costs and Benefits of Leveraged ETFs
nominations.authors: Chris Murray, Marco Sammon
nominations.abstract: We study the costs and benefits of leveraged ETFs (LETFs), focusing on five determinants of performance: volatility drag, fees, financing costs, which products are launched, and market timing. Long broad-equity-index LETFs generated more than $100 billion in investor gains, including over $40 billion relative to counterfactual investments in the underlying assets, due to modest structural headwinds and rising markets. Single-stock LETFs, however, are launched on stocks near the top of the volatility and past-return distributions. This caters to retail demand for lottery-like payoffs, but it also creates larger volatility drag, higher financing costs, and more risk for poor market-timing.

nominations.title: Social Networks and the Propagation of Household Shocks to Asset Prices
nominations.authors: Faisal Quaiyyum
nominations.abstract: When can local household disturbances move credit prices? I develop a financially weighted propagation operator on the social network. In a conditional household-intermediary equilibrium, its projection determines the household-demand component of the excess bond premium. Because responses decay at different rates across network patterns and channels, a location's relative financial importance generically changes with the horizon, so no single centrality measure summarizes exposure across horizons. Household measurements recover this projection exactly when they span independently measured demand sensitivities. Empirically, social exposure to storm-damaged counties is negatively associated with spending weeks later in counties outside the recorded footprints. In simulations on the observed network under the model's diffusion law, the operator predicts the propagated credit-premium component of held-out storms with about 30 percent less error than direct social exposure.

nominations.title: Same Text, Different Filename: Are LLM Judges Biased?
nominations.authors: Sergey V. Popov
nominations.abstract: Yes. In 2026, leading economic journals started using Refine.ink in the technical quality assessment of submissions before publication. I study whether renaming a file changes the perception of the document's quality by LLM judges. I find that three frontier LLMs score the same document differently if you change the document's filename. A person-related label scores higher than no label; there is no consistent preference of own- or rival-based label, nor a penalty for an Asian name, but there is a context-specific bias in assessments whose direction and size vary with both document and label. With LLM-written documents, some self-premium can be detected, but a significant context-dependent label bias remains. Whether to combat it is a question of the costs of evaluation errors.

nominations.title: Owning What Can Quit
nominations.authors: Douglas Cumming
nominations.abstract: Academic journals are part of the infrastructure of science, yet most journal titles are owned by commercial publishers while their standing rests on editors and boards who can leave. This paper asks what that separation means for the governance of science. Using a coded dataset of all 57 editorial mass resignations recorded by Retraction Watch from 2015 to 2026, data on editor tenure at 110 economics, finance and accounting journals, and journal-level publication and revenue data, I document three patterns. First, resignation does not reverse an owner's decision: in none of the 19 episodes involving an editor's replacement did the owner back down after the board resigned, so editorial communities have influence only before they leave.
